detail.extracted_title: Drones Over the Wadi, GIS in the Classroom: How Omani Students Are Mapping Their Own Communities
detail.excerpt: From charting falaj water channels and heritage trails in Samail to tracking urban expansion in Al Mabelah, Omani geography teachers and students are turning satellite data into local civic planning.
detail.article_html:
In a computer room at Bilal bin Rabah Boys' School (Grades 5–12) in Ad Dakhiliyah Governorate, students are not memorizing capitals from a paper wall map. Instead, they are layering multi-year satellite imagery over digital elevation models in QGIS and Google Earth—tracing how seasonal wadi runoff intersects with expanding residential neighborhoods, and pinpointing where flash-flood channels require wider buffer zones.

Across Oman's governorates, the school geography classroom has undergone a quiet transformation. Celebrated during Geographic Awareness Week—held from November 16 to 20 across the Ministry of Education's directorates—hundreds of Omani students are using Geographic Information Systems (GIS), unmanned aerial vehicle (drone) surveys, remote sensing, and 3D digital models to study the real physical challenges of their own towns.

From Passive Map Readers to Spatial Investigators

As Abdullah bin Khalaf Al Rawahi, Senior Geography Teacher at Bilal bin Rabah School and a member of Ad Dakhiliyah's geographic technology team (Techno-Map), observes, putting live spatial data in front of a teenager changes how they see their own village. When a student compares satellite images of the same agricultural plain taken ten years apart, or overlays slope gradients onto wadi beds and housing clusters, a map stops being a flat picture and becomes an analytical database.

In the Wilayat of Samail, Al Rawahi's students took that approach out into the field. Combining GPS coordinates, aerial photography, and GIS layers, they mapped Samail's historic watchtowers, forts, and tourist sites—designing interactive heritage trails and proposing new visitor service points to support local tourism. In a parallel field investigation, students used satellite imagery to audit water resources across Samail's traditional aflaj channels and analyze how seasonal wadi flows affect nearby roads and buildings, recommending safer zones for future residential expansion.

Tracking Urban Growth in Al Mabelah and Founding "Arth"

Closer to the coast in Muscat Governorate, students at Al Mabelah South Girls' School (Grades 10–12) have turned remote sensing toward rapid urban growth. Under the guidance of Senior Geography Teacher Munira bint Nasser Al Malki, students compared historical and current satellite imagery of Al Mabelah to measure how residential blocks have expanded over former open plains—translating raw census and municipal tables into interactive thematic maps that show where green spaces, school services, and road corridors are most needed.

That classroom momentum even sparked a student-run startup. Students at the school founded a digital tourism company called "Arth," building an interactive spatial platform that uses GIS and artificial intelligence tools to document Omani architectural heritage and guide visitors to historical landmarks across the Sultanate.

Meanwhile, at Umm Saad Al Ansariya School (Grades 7–10), social studies teacher Hiba bint Mohammed Al Hammadi uses digital relief maps to help younger students answer fundamental questions about Oman's human geography: why ancient settlements clustered along specific mountain piedmonts, how limestone topography dictates modern highway engineering, and how coastal plains interact with monsoon moisture.

Offline Field Kits and the National Digital Educational Atlas

In rural and mountain wilayats where high-speed internet inside a classroom cannot always be taken for granted, teachers have adapted with practical ingenuity. At Hai Al Turath Basic Education School (Grades 9–12), Senior Geography Teacher Mohammed bin Saif Al Busaidi compiles localized offline GIS datasets and high-resolution aerial tiles so students can run spatial analysis without needing a live internet connection. Further east in South Al Sharqiyah Governorate, geography teacher Ali bin Said Al Musharrafi at Uqba bin Nafi School guides students through MapWindows and Google Earth workshops to author their own statistical reports before entering national research competitions.

According to Khalid bin Ahmed Al Kalbani, Cartography Specialist and Head of the Central Technical Team for Modern Geographic Technologies at the Ministry of Education's Directorate General of Curriculum Development, these school projects are now anchored by a nationwide infrastructure push. Alongside equipping dedicated school geography laboratories and training teachers in spatial AI, the Ministry has completed the Digital Educational Atlas of the Sultanate of Oman—giving every teacher and student a standardized, authoritative spatial database of their country's terrain, climate, water networks, and settlements.

detail.instagram_caption:
Across Oman's governorates, school geography has moved far beyond memorizing paper maps. Using Geographic Information Systems (GIS) like QGIS and Google Earth, drone aerial surveys, and multi-year satellite imagery, Omani students are conducting field investigations into the real planning challenges of their own wilayats.

In Ad Dakhiliyah Governorate, students at Bilal bin Rabah Boys' School in Samail have used GIS and aerial photography to map historic landmarks, design tourist service routes, track falaj water regression, and model wadi flood risks to recommend safer zones for residential construction. In Muscat, students at Al Mabelah South Girls' School analyzed satellite archives to trace rapid urban expansion and even launched a student digital tourism company called "Arth" using spatial AI to showcase Omani heritage.

Backed by the Ministry of Education's newly completed Digital Educational Atlas of the Sultanate of Oman and specialized school geography labs, educators from Nizwa to South Al Sharqiyah are equipping a new generation of Omani spatial thinkers to read—and protect—their own terrain.
